rows.selection_reason: No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence to exploit; the priority is establishing a clean, interpretable baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest standard configuration: PCA is the most widely used and reproducible RNA dimensionality reduction, single-profile avoids confounding from aggregation, and RNA-only avoids confounding from fusion. This experiment establishes (1) whether the RNA signal alone is informative for the task, (2) a performance floor against which all image-only, multimodal, and alternative-encoder configurations can be compared, and (3) a reference for how much value the more complex design choices (scvi, scgpt, multiprofile, image, fusion) actually add. Under a limited budget, anchoring the search with the most standard, low-risk baseline maximizes the interpretability of every subsequent comparison and reduces uncertainty about whether the task is solvable from RNA at all before investing experiments in more complex modalities or encoders.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), evidence is extremely sparse and the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries independent predictive signal. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean, single-axis comparison to config_001 that isolates modality: it keeps the same profile setting and simplicity level (no aggregation, no fusion) while swapping RNA for image. If image_only performs comparably or better, it validates pursuing multimodal fusion; if it performs poorly, it signals that image adds little and we should focus budget on RNA encoder or profile improvements. Answering this foundational question before investing in any multimodal or multiprofile configuration maximizes information per experiment and prevents misattributing performance gains/losses in later fusion experiments.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieved 0.485 acc / 0.464 F1, while config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) was much weaker at 0.208 acc / 0.172 F1. RNA is clearly the dominant modality, but we have only tested one RNA encoder (PCA). Uncertainty: whether a learned, biologically-informed encoder (scVI) substantially outperforms linear PCA for downstream classification. This experiment (config_004: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) makes the minimal single-variable change from our best baseline—swapping only the RNA encoder while holding profile setting and all other hyperparameters constant. It cleanly isolates the encoder effect. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) it directly answers whether representation quality is a major performance lever, which would inform every subsequent multimodal and multiprofile experiment; (2) if scVI is markedly better, we gain a stronger RNA backbone to build on; if similar, PCA suffices and we can focus budget on profile/aggregation/fusion axes; (3) it avoids conflating multiple design choices, keeping the comparison interpretable under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA-only models clearly dominate (0.485–0.520) over image-only (0.208), and among RNA encoders, scvi_n200 (0.520) outperforms pca_n2000 (0.485) in singleprofile rna_only settings. However, scgpt remains untested, leaving uncertainty about which RNA representation is best. Question: config_007 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) provides a clean, single-variable comparison against config_001 (pca) and config_004 (scvi), isolating the effect of the RNA encoder while holding profile setting and modality constant. Why this is the best next experiment: Resolving the encoder question before investing in multiprofile or multimodal configurations avoids committing the remaining budget to a suboptimal representation. If scgpt is substantially better, it reshapes the entire search; if it is comparable or worse, we can confidently build forward with scvi_n200. This is the highest-information experiment given the current sparse evidence.

Evidence: All four completed experiments are singleprofile. The best result is config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) at 0.520 acc, establishing scvi_n200 as the strongest RNA encoder. Image-only (resnet50) is very weak (0.208), reducing the urgency of multimodal tests. The largest remaining uncertainty is whether multiprofile aggregation provides meaningful gains over singleprofile. Question: Does multiprofile with the best RNA encoder (scvi_n200) improve validation accuracy over the 0.520 singleprofile baseline? config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) isolates the profile-setting effect while using the simplest aggregation (avgpool), avoiding confounding from a more complex transformer. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly tests the most impactful unexplored design axis (profile setting) with the best-known encoder, and the result will inform whether to invest further in multiprofile variants or pivot to other axes.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc, a large jump over its singleprofile counterpart config_004 (0.520), making it the clear best configuration so far. The dominant design axis is now RNA encoder + multiprofile setting. Uncertainty: we have not tested whether transformer aggregation outperforms avgpool under this strong setting. This experiment (config_006) isolates the aggregation choice (transformer vs avgpool) while holding rna_only, scvi_n200, and multiprofile fixed—a clean single-variable comparison directly extending our strongest result. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it exploits the most promising direction with a minimal, interpretable change, and the answer (whether transformer adds value over simple averaging) will guide all subsequent multiprofile and multimodal experiments that involve aggregation.

Evidence: The largest effect observed so far is the multiprofile boost for scvi_n200 (0.520 single → 0.650/0.653 multi, ~+13 pts), while singleprofile RNA encoders rank scvi_n200 > pca_n2000 > scgpt. Image-only (resnet50) is essentially at chance (0.208). Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the multiprofile gain is a general property of seeing multiple profiles or is specific to scvi's learned latent representation. Question: config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) directly tests this by changing only the profile setting from config_001 (pca, single: 0.485). If pca also jumps substantially, multiprofile is a universal design lever; if it stays near 0.485, the gain is tied to scvi's learned representation. This is the best next experiment because it isolates one variable (profile setting) against an already-completed baseline, reduces uncertainty about a core architectural decision before committing budget to multimodal or additional encoder combinations, and the aggregation choice (avgpool) is already shown to be near-equivalent to transformer, so it does not confound the comparison.

Evidence: The best RNA-only configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) achieves 0.653 accuracy, while the only image-only test (resnet50, singleprofile) scored a very weak 0.208. This single data point is insufficient to conclude the image modality carries no signal—resnet50 may simply be a poor encoder for this task. Uncertainty: Before investing budget in any multimodal fusion configuration, we need to know whether a stronger image encoder (ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L) can extract meaningful cellular signal. This experiment tests exactly that: image-only with ViT-L in a clean singleprofile setting, isolating the encoder choice. Why this is the best next step: If ViT-L also performs poorly, we can confidently redirect remaining budget to RNA-only optimization (e.g., exploring scgpt+multi or confirming aggregation effects). If ViT-L performs substantially better than resnet50, it justifies the next experiments in multimodal fusion with the best RNA encoder. This single experiment resolves the largest open design question—whether the image modality is worth pursuing at all—without changing multiple variables simultaneously.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 is the strongest configuration (0.653 acc / 0.628 F1, config_006), and image-only models are very weak (best: ViT-L at 0.227 acc, config_013). The single biggest design lever identified is multiprofile (+13 pts over single-profile), and scvi_n200 is the best RNA encoder. The critical remaining uncertainty is whether fusing the weak image signal with the strong RNA signal adds any value. This experiment (config_039) pairs the best RNA encoder (scvi_n200), best image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), multiprofile, transformer aggregation, and weighted fusion—directly testing whether weighted multimodal fusion can improve on the 0.653 RNA-only baseline. Weighted fusion is chosen over concat because it can learn to downweight a weak modality, making it the most informative test: if even weighted fusion fails to beat the RNA-only result, it provides strong evidence that image contributes little and further multimodal exploration is not worthwhile under a limited budget. This single experiment resolves the highest-impact open design question before committing additional budget to the 20+ remaining multimodal configurations.

Evidence: config_039 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + transformer + weighted fusion) achieved 0.725 acc, the best result so far, a substantial jump over the best RNA-only multiprofile (0.653, config_006). However, we have only one multimodal data point, so we cannot yet tell whether the weighted fusion specifically drives this gain or whether any fusion would work. Question: config_038 is identical to config_039 except fusion changes from weighted to concat, cleanly isolating the fusion-method effect. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a minimal, single-variable comparison that directly tests whether the fusion strategy is a critical design decision or interchangeable. If concat performs similarly, the fusion choice is a low-priority axis and we can focus budget on image-encoder or aggregation effects. If concat is substantially worse, it confirms weighted fusion as a necessary component and guides all future multimodal experiments. This is more informative than testing a second image encoder or aggregation variant, because fusion is the mechanism by which the two modalities interact and we have zero prior evidence on it.
